Secemin Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Secemin, Poland

Demolished. Secemin was an important center of the Protestant Reformation in the 16th and early 17th centuries, and its Jewish community, present from the 16th century, endured a documented blood libel trial in 1649. By 1739, Jews owned about a quarter of the town's plots; an independent kehilla was active by 1765, though the cemetery itself likely predates that, established around the turn of the 18th century. It fell out of use no later than 1920, and after Secemin's Jews became administratively subordinate to the kehilla in nearby Włoszczowa in 1867, they were deported to the Włoszczowa Ghetto in the summer of 1942. According to testimony from Jan Lochmann, about 20 matzevot remained visible in the already-closed cemetery during the interwar period; during the war, the site was used for executions, and afterward an agricultural cooperative developed the grounds. No tombstones survive, and the site remains unmarked today.
